title: Valid Sudoku
summary: You get a 9×9 Sudoku grid `board`, partly filled: each cell holds a digit from "1" to "9" or "." for an empty cell. Decide whether the digits placed so far break a rule: no digit may appear twice in the same row, the same column, or the same 3×3 box. You don't need to check whether the puzzle can be solved; only the filled cells count.

examples.explanation: Sixteen digits, and none repeats within a row, a column or a 3×3 box.
The 3 at row 1, column 1 shares the top-left box with the 3 at row 0, column 2, though they sit in different rows and columns.

constraints: board[r][c] is a digit from "1" to "9" or "."

approaches.twist: Record each filled cell's digit under its row, its column and its box (r // 3, c // 3) in sets; a repeat breaks the rule.
For each filled cell, scan its whole row, column and box for another cell with the same digit.
approaches.note: Works, and the board is small, but each cell scans up to 3n others: O(n³) for an n×n board. A set per row, column and box answers each check in O(1).

signals.meaning: A repeat check: remember the digits you've met and look each new one up. Here there are 27 places to remember them in: 9 rows, 9 columns and 9 boxes.
Cell (r, c) lies in box (r // 3, c // 3). That pair is the key for the box's set, so no box needs a loop of its own.
A list of lists: board[r][c] is row r, column c. enumerate gives you both the index and the cell.

constraintReading: The board is always 9×9, so even a slow check finishes at once; what's tested is the method. Measured by the side n = 9, one pass over the n² cells with an O(1) set lookup per cell is O(n²) time, and the sets hold at most 3 entries per cell, O(n²) space. Scanning a row, a column and a box for every cell is O(n³).

hints.clarify: Does an empty cell count? No: only digits do, and a board can be valid even if it can't be solved. Which cells share a box? Rows 0–2 with columns 0–2 form the first box, rows 0–2 with columns 3–5 the next, and so on. So a "5" at row 1, column 4 and another "5" at row 2, column 3 clash, though they're in different rows and columns.
hints.approach: Hash sets of what's been seen. Walk the board once. For each filled cell, the digit claims three places: its row r, its column c and its box (r // 3, c // 3). Give each claim a key, such as "5 in row 1" or "5 in box 0-1", and keep every key in one set. If a key is already there, an earlier cell made the same claim, so the board breaks a rule. If every key is new, the board is valid.
hints.whyNot: Scanning the row, column and box of every filled cell works, but it reads up to 27 cells per cell, O(n³) for an n×n board. Checking the 9 rows, then the 9 columns, then the 9 boxes, each with a fresh set, is also O(n²) but walks the board three times and needs separate loop code for boxes; one pass with three keys per cell is shorter.

slots.setup: One empty set `seen` for every claim made so far, written as a string such as "5 in col 3". Three sets per row, column and box work just as well.
slots.loop: Visit every cell once: rows with `enumerate(board)`, then the cells of each row. Skip a ".".
slots.update: When a claim is new, add its key to `seen`, so a later cell with the same digit in the same row, column or box finds it.
slots.record: Build the three keys for the digit: its row, its column, and its box `r // 3`, `c // 3`. Look each one up in `seen` first; a hit means the digit appears twice in that row, column or box.
slots.return: Return false on the first hit. If every filled cell is visited without one, return true.

solution.explanation: Each of the n² cells is visited once, and a filled cell does three set lookups and adds: O(n²) time, 81 cells for a real board. The set holds three keys per filled cell, at most 3n² keys: O(n²) space. The box key is the pair (r // 3, c // 3): integer division maps rows 0–2 to 0, rows 3–5 to 1 and rows 6–8 to 2, and columns the same way, so each of the nine boxes gets its own name.

events.label: claim
events.say: board[{r}][{c}] is {d}. It claims {d} for row {r}, column {c} and box {r // 3}-{c // 3}

events.label: repeat
events.say: {key!r} is already in seen: an earlier {d} made the same claim, so the board is invalid

events.label: return
events.say: Every filled cell made only new claims, so no digit repeats: the board is valid

predict.ask: Will this digit clash with one placed earlier?
predict.answerWhen: f'{d} in row {r}' in seen or f'{d} in col {c}' in seen or f'{d} in box {r // 3}-{c // 3}' in seen

predict.ask: Will this digit clash with one placed earlier?
predict.answerWhen: f'{d} in row {r}' in seen or f'{d} in col {c}' in seen or f'{d} in box {r // 3}-{c // 3}' in seen

related.relation: The same repeat check with a set, on one list instead of 27 overlapping groups of cells.
Also builds a key that names an item's group, a sorted word there and a row, column or box here.
